title: How Rice Gets to the Bowl
learning_objectives: Follow a process with several stages in order
Learn the words seedling, paddy, harvest and husk in context

factual_claims.claim: Rice is a grass; the grains we eat are its seeds.
factual_claims.source: Britannica, 'Rice' (rice is a cereal grass); International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) Rice Knowledge Bank

factual_claims.claim: Rice seeds are often sprouted in a nursery bed and the young seedlings transplanted into flooded fields (paddies).
Rice plants grow well standing in shallow water, which also keeps down many weeds.
factual_claims.source: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank, 'Water management'; Britannica, 'Rice'

factual_claims.claim: Rice takes roughly three to six months from planting to harvest depending on the variety.
factual_claims.source: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank, 'Growth stages of the rice plant' (90-180 days)

factual_claims.claim: After harvest, grains are dried and the hard outer husk is removed (milling) before the rice is cooked.
Rice is a staple food for more than half of the world's people.

parent_prompts: Before: where does the rice in your bowl come from? What did it look like before?
After page 5: why do the fields have water in them?
After: which stage do you think is the hardest work?

pages.text: There is rice in your bowl tonight. Small, white, soft. But a few months ago, every one of those grains was a seed in the mud. This is the journey it took.
pages.illustration_brief: A bowl of white rice with steam; behind it, faded, a green paddy field.
pages.audio_script: There is rice in your bowl tonight. Small, white, soft. But a few months ago, every one of those grains was a seed in the mud. This is the journey it took.
pages.image_alt: A bowl of white rice with steam; behind it, faded, a green paddy field.

pages.text: Rice is a kind of grass. The grains are its seeds. Farmers keep some seeds from last year and soak them in water until tiny roots and shoots appear.
pages.illustration_brief: A shallow tray of rice seeds, some with tiny white roots and green shoots.
pages.audio_script: Rice is a kind of grass. The grains are its seeds. Farmers keep some seeds from last year and soak them in water until tiny roots and shoots appear.
pages.image_alt: A shallow tray of rice seeds, some with tiny white roots and green shoots.

pages.text: The sprouted seeds are planted close together in a small muddy bed. In a few weeks they are bright green seedlings as long as your hand.
pages.illustration_brief: A dense square of bright green seedlings in mud, a hand beside for scale.
pages.audio_script: The sprouted seeds are planted close together in a small muddy bed. In a few weeks they are bright green seedlings as long as your hand.

vocabulary.definition: A very young plant that has just grown from a seed.
vocabulary.example: The tomato seedling has two leaves.

pages.image_alt: A dense square of bright green seedlings in mud, a hand beside for scale.

pages.text: Now comes the hard part. Farmers pull up the seedlings in bunches and walk into the big field, which is flooded with shallow water. Bending low, they push each seedling into the mud, one by one, in long straight rows.
pages.illustration_brief: Farmers in conical hats bent over in a flooded field, planting rows of seedlings; reflections in the water.
pages.audio_script: Now comes the hard part. Farmers pull up the seedlings in bunches and walk into the big field, which is flooded with shallow water. Bending low, they push each seedling into the mud, one by one, in long straight rows.

vocabulary.definition: A field flooded with water where rice grows.
vocabulary.example: Ducks swim between the rice plants in the paddy.

pages.image_alt: Farmers in conical hats bent over in a flooded field, planting rows of seedlings.

pages.text: Why the water? Rice likes wet feet. The water also drowns most weeds, so the rice does not have to share the sun. Frogs, small fish and dragonflies move in too.
pages.illustration_brief: Close view of rice stems standing in water; a frog on a stem, a dragonfly above, small fish below.
pages.audio_script: Why the water? Rice likes wet feet. The water also drowns most weeds, so the rice does not have to share the sun. Frogs, small fish and dragonflies move in too.
pages.image_alt: Close view of rice stems standing in water; a frog on a stem, a dragonfly above, small fish below.

pages.text: For three or four months the plants grow tall. Then they flower, and each flower becomes a grain. The heads get heavy and bend over, and the whole field turns from green to gold.
pages.illustration_brief: A golden field of rice with heavy drooping heads; one head shown close with many grains.
pages.audio_script: For three or four months the plants grow tall. Then they flower, and each flower becomes a grain. The heads get heavy and bend over, and the whole field turns from green to gold.
pages.image_alt: A golden field of rice with heavy drooping heads; one head shown close with many grains.

pages.text: Harvest time. The stalks are cut and the grains are shaken loose. They are spread in the sun to dry, sometimes right on the road, raked into long golden stripes.
pages.illustration_brief: Rice grains spread on a road drying, a person raking them into stripes; cut stalks in bundles behind.
pages.audio_script: Harvest time. The stalks are cut and the grains are shaken loose. They are spread in the sun to dry, sometimes right on the road, raked into long golden stripes.

vocabulary.definition: Gathering crops when they are ripe.
vocabulary.example: The apple harvest is in autumn.

pages.image_alt: Rice grains spread on a road drying, a person raking them into stripes.

pages.text: Each grain still wears a hard brown coat called the husk. A machine rubs the husks off. Underneath is the white rice you know.
pages.illustration_brief: Left: brown husked grains; right: white polished grains; a simple milling machine between.
pages.audio_script: Each grain still wears a hard brown coat called the husk. A machine rubs the husks off. Underneath is the white rice you know.

vocabulary.definition: The hard dry outer coat of a seed or grain.
vocabulary.example: Peel the husk off the corn.

pages.image_alt: Left: brown husked grains; right: white polished grains; a simple milling machine between.

pages.text: Seed, seedling, paddy, gold, harvest, husk. Then a bag, a shop, a pot, and your bowl. More than half the people in the world eat rice every day. Tonight, you are one of them.
pages.illustration_brief: A row of small icons: seed, seedling, paddy, golden head, grain pile, bowl; a child eating rice at the end.
pages.audio_script: Seed, seedling, paddy, gold, harvest, husk. Then a bag, a shop, a pot, and your bowl. More than half the people in the world eat rice every day. Tonight, you are one of them.
